newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Weathermen forecast no drought in Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: Weathermen forecast no drought in Sri Lanka.

text.p: Sri Lankan weathermen said on Friday they feared no repetition of last year's crippling drought despite only a trickle of rainfall last month.

Rainfall in January was just 1.3 mm (0.05 inches) compared with 157.3 mm (6.2 inches) in January 1996 in Nuwara Eliya, the main central hill and reservoir district, a Meteorological Department official said.
"But these figures should not be taken in isolation, since January and February are usually very dry months," deputy director Jayatilaka Banda said.

He also said that despite good rains in January 1996, the country was gripped by a crippling drought, due to failure of intermonsoon rains in March and a delay in the onset of the southwest monsoon in late May.
"However, we do not expect a drought this year, since according to current weather patterns, intermonsoon rains and the southwest monsoon should come on time," Banda said.

The country's power utility company, the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), said it has increased output from thermal power plants until May to compensate for lower reseroir levels at hydro power stations during the dry period.
"We are now generating about 210 megawatts of thermal power, whereas we had only about 150 megawatts of thermal power at the same time last year," said a CEB official who declined to be named.
Sri Lanka, which has depended on hydro power for 84 percent of its total power needs of 1,345 megawatts, hopes to cut dependence to 50 percent by 2000.
Of the current total thermal power output, about 150 megawatts are from plants in the Colombo suburbs of Sapugaskande and Kelanitissa, while the rest comes from private plants, the CEB official said.
The country saw one of the worst droughts in recent history in 1996, when failure of monsoon rains led to daily power cuts averaging five hours from March to August.
"Even though water levels at reservoirs are now at about 46 percent of capacity, increased thermal power generation should see us through if there is a drought this year," the CEB official said.
Sri Lanka's two main export crops, tea and rubber, have already been affected by the current dry season, analysts said.
"Despite the current dry season, volumes of tea auctioned in Colombo are being maintained only because of a backlog from December," said Anil Cooke of produce brokers Forbes & Walker.
Rubber prices at Colombo auctions this week were high due to drought fears and strong overseas demand, brokers said.
